name: Cable Shrug

inherit.why: true for this child because the Baechle and Earle rule covers all grips (see the thumb claim).
true for this child because it is the same hold archetype with the load hanging from straight arms; same O’Driscoll 1992 cue (see the wrist claim).
true for this child because heavy shrugs are also heavy lifts; same MacDougall 1985 line.
true for this child because the shoulder is loaded the same way; same shoulder box (Kolber 2010). Neck rows link no box (content.md 5.3).
true for this child because the cable bar is also held palms down (c1).

claims.text: Take a straight bar on a low pulley, hands about shoulder width or slightly wider, palms facing down.

quotes.text: Grab a cable bar attachment that is fastened to a low pulley. Your hands should be shoulder width apart, or slightly wider if you wish. Your hands should be facing down.

claims.text: Stand close to the pulley with the arms extended in front holding the bar; that is the start.

quotes.text: Stand close to the pulley and extend your arms in front of you while holding the bar. This is the starting position.

claims.text: Elevate the shoulders to lift the bar as high as possible, breathing out, and hold the top for a second.

quotes.text: Elevating your shoulders, lift the bar as high as you possibly can. Exhale while performing this motion. Hold the contraction at the top for a second.

claims.text: Stand up straight, head up, eyes forward.

quotes.text: Stand up straight while performing the exercise.
Keep your head up and eyes facing forward throughout.

claims.text: Do not lift the bar with the biceps; only the shoulders move up and down.

quotes.text: Do not use your biceps to lift the bar. Your shoulders should be the only part of your body moving up and down during the exercise.

claims.text: Lower the bar back to the start.

quotes.text: Lower the bar to its original position.

claims.text: Tempo: about 1-2 s up and 1-2 s down, with a one-second hold at the top. ACSM gives its 1-2 s each way for intermediate to advanced lifters working toward heavy loads, so the up and down seconds are a drawing convention; the 1 s top hold is sourced.

quotes.text: For intermediate (individuals with approximately 6 months of consistent RT experience) to advanced (individuals with years of RT experience) training
with eventual emphasis on heavy loading (1-6 RM) using 3- to 5-min rest periods between sets performed at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
Hold the contraction at the top for a second.

claims.text: The shrug is an isolation exercise for the muscles that lift the shoulder girdle, such as the upper trapezius (barbell source; same movement on a cable).

quotes.text: The shrug is an isolation exercise for the muscles that lifts and supports your shoulder girdle, like the top portion of your trapezius among others.

claims.text: Raise the shoulders straight up toward the ears as high as possible, then lower; do not roll them (ACE barbell shrug page; same shoulder movement on a cable).

quotes.text: raise the shoulders directly upwards to the ears as high as possible
focus on only raising/lowering the shoulders - DO NOT roll the shoulders.

claims.text: Wrap the thumbs around the handle or bar.

quotes.text: Perform all grips with your thumbs around the bar.

claims.text: Grip is strongest with the wrist in its natural extended (bent-back) position, about 35 degrees, and weakens when the wrist moves away from it, even to 15 degrees of extension (measured on grip, applied here as a wrist cue).

quotes.text: Grip strength is significantly reduced when wrist position deviates from this self-selected optimum position.
The self-selected position was 35 degrees of extension and 7 degrees of ulnar deviation.
With the wrist in only 15 degrees of extension or in neutral radio-ulnar deviation, grip strength was reduced to two thirds to three fourths of normal.

claims.text: Add load in small steps (2-10%) only once the target reps are exceeded by one or two.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Heavy lifting with a held breath (Valsalva) drives blood pressure very high.

quotes.text: It was concluded that when healthy young subjects perform weight-lifting exercises the mechanical compression of blood vessels combines with a potent pressor response and a Valsalva response to produce extreme elevations in blood pressure.

claims.text: The shoulder is one of the most common injury sites in resistance training (up to 36% of documented injuries), and poor technique is a named risk factor.

quotes.text: The results of the review indicated that up to 36% of documented RT-related injuries and disorders occur at the shoulder complex.
extrinsic risk factors, namely, that of improper attention to exercise technique.

claims.text: In EMG studies the shrug gives very high upper-trapezius activity: the one-arm shrug was the highest of ten exercises in healthy adults, and the shrug the highest of five in women with neck muscle pain (implement not stated in either abstract).

quotes.text: The unilateral shoulder shrug exercise was found to produce the greatest EMG activity in the upper trapezius.
For the trapezius muscle, the highest level of muscle activation was found during the shrug (102+/-11% of MVC), lateral raise (97+/-6% of MVC), and upright row (85+/-5% of MVC) exercises

claims.text: The lowering is slow, back to the starting position (from the ACE barbell shrug page; same shoulder movement on a cable).

quotes.text: lowering slowly to the original starting position.

plate.viewWhy: Straight arms, the upright body and the straight-up shoulder path read side-on (c2, c4, c5); the census draws it side, like the parent.
plate.equipment: Cable column with the pulley at the bottom; straight bar held in front of the thighs, lifter standing close to the column so the cable runs nearly straight down (c1, c2); floor line.
plate.start: Standing up straight, head up (c4), arms extended holding the bar in front (c2), shoulders relaxed down.
plate.end: Same body; shoulders lifted as high as they go (c3), arms still straight (c5).

checkpoints.label: Straight arms
checkpoints.what: The biceps don’t lift. Only the shoulders move.

checkpoints.label: Stand straight
checkpoints.what: Upright body, head up, eyes forward.

checkpoints.label: Hold the top
checkpoints.what: One-second hold with the shoulders up.

mistake.what: Elbows bend to curl the bar up instead of the shoulders lifting it.
mistake.why: The anchor’s first tip names it (c5); bent arms are visible side-on. Rolling (c9) cannot be drawn.
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 3, then LR-36: the arms bending to lift the bar (c5). Step 1: no frequency word counts for a fault. Set aside: StrengthLog's "Dumbbells, barbell, and trap bar are all common tools for this exercise." (the equipment); Kolber's "the most prevalent regions of injury" (where injuries happen, no fault) and "A majority of the available research was retrospective" (the research). Step 2: no quote ties a named fault to harm; Kolber's "improper attention to exercise technique" (c14) names no fault. Step 3: no read source has a common-mistakes list. Two faults are each one source's "avoid": the biceps lifting the bar (Exercise.com: "Do not use your biceps to lift the bar.", c5) and rolling the shoulders (ACE, for the barbell shrug: "DO NOT roll the shoulders.", c9). StrengthLog's "Hold a barbell in straight arms in front of your body." and Exercise.com's "Stand up straight while performing the exercise." are instructions, not faults to avoid. Tie ruled by the supervisor (LR-36): the head's pick stays because the census view was chosen for it; LR-31 gives no further order. plate.viewWhy names the straight arms (c5) that the bent arms break. drawable stays true: the side view shows the bent elbows, a still sign. Pick unchanged.

tempo.text: Pause 1 s at the top: Exercise.com's "Hold the contraction at the top for a second." (c3, c7) is right after the lift and gives its seconds (LR-33). Up 1 and down 2 keep ACSM's 1-2 s, stated for intermediate to advanced training (c7, WEAK; LR-15); ACE asks for "lowering slowly to the original starting position" (c16).

grip.type: Overhand (palms down) on a straight cable bar.
grip.handContact: Bar across the middle of the palm, fingers wrapped (hold archetype).
grip.wrist: Bent back into its natural grip position (about 35 degrees), not curled forward; grip weakens when the wrist moves away from it.

setup.step: Straight bar on the low pulley.
Overhand grip, hands shoulder width or a little wider.
Stand close to the pulley, arms straight, bar in front of you.

posture.point: Stand up straight the whole set.
Arms straight. Only the shoulders move.
Up and down only, no rolling.
Hold the top for a second, lower slowly.

handlingMistakes.fix: Stand up straight, head up, eyes forward.

rows.where: Top of shoulders, beside the neck
rows.means: The upper traps do the lifting.
Fault: bending the arms to lift the bar.
Poor technique is a risk for shoulder injuries.
rows.fix: Stop the set. Don't train through the pain.

risks.risk: Holding your breath hard on heavy reps sends blood pressure very high.
The shoulder is a common injury site in weight training. Poor technique adds risk.

zooms.right: Wrist bent back, in its natural grip position.
Shoulders up, arms straight, standing straight.
zooms.wrong: Elbows bent, curling the bar up.

libraryDiff.why: Library primary upper_traps matches (c8, c15). The anchor names no other muscle.
